technique.how: Inspect and palpate the supine abdomen for distension, tenseness (drum-like resistance to gentle pressure), tympany and tenderness; note girth, wound/fascial tension, high ventilator pressures, oliguria and vasopressor need. Record a global judgment 'abdominal pressure elevated vs normal', then confirm with intravesical (bladder) pressure measurement.
technique.prerequisites: Know risk factors: massive resuscitation, laparotomy, pancreatitis, ascites, ileus, burns, obesity, high PEEP.
technique.contraindications: None for examination; bladder pressure requires a urinary catheter.

interpretation.positive_finding: An abdomen judged tense/distended in a critically ill patient raises the probability of elevated IAP (LR+ ≈6.7 for bladder pressure >10 mm Hg, ≈4.3 for >15 mm Hg) and mandates a bladder-pressure measurement. Combined with new organ dysfunction (AKI, high airway pressures) consider abdominal compartment syndrome.
interpretation.negative_finding: A soft or non-distended abdomen does not exclude intra-abdominal hypertension (sensitivity 40–56%; LR− 0.5–0.6). Measure bladder pressure in any at-risk ICU patient with oliguria or rising ventilator pressures.
interpretation.pitfalls: Examination was compared with bladder pressure, the reference used by WSACS; thresholds in the study (>10, >15 mm Hg) differ from the WSACS definition (IAH = sustained IAP ≥12 mm Hg, ACS >20 mm Hg with organ failure). Obesity, ascites and open abdomens confound both exam and pressure.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive → measure bladder pressure now and treat IAH (decompress gut/ascites, sedation, fluid balance); negative in at-risk ICU patient → still measure.

estimates.target_condition: Elevated intra-abdominal pressure, bladder pressure >10 mm Hg — index test: blinded clinician judgment of abdominal pressure as 'elevated' on examination
estimates.population: 42 adult blunt-trauma ICU patients (mean ISS 36); 147 paired daily bladder-pressure measurements and blinded examinations (measurement-level analysis)
estimates.computed_from: LRs computed from reported sensitivity 40% and specificity 94%: LR+ = 0.40/0.06 = 6.7; LR− = 0.60/0.94 = 0.64. Prevalence = 47/147 measurements >10 mm Hg.
estimates.quote: accuracy of clinical abdominal examination for identifying elevated IAP were 40%, 94%, 76%, 77% and 77%, respectively

estimates.target_condition: Significantly elevated intra-abdominal pressure, bladder pressure >15 mm Hg — index test: blinded clinician judgment of abdominal pressure as 'elevated' on examination
estimates.population: 42 adult blunt-trauma ICU patients (mean ISS 36); 147 paired daily bladder-pressure measurements and blinded examinations (measurement-level analysis)
estimates.computed_from: LRs computed from reported sensitivity 56% and specificity 87%: LR+ = 0.56/0.13 = 4.3; LR− = 0.44/0.87 = 0.51. Prevalence = 16/147 measurements >15 mm Hg.
estimates.quote: accuracy of 56%, 87%, 35%, 94% and 84% respectively, for significantly elevated IAP

sources.citation: Kirkpatrick AW, Brenneman FD, McLean RF, Rapanos T, Boulanger BR. Is clinical examination an accurate indicator of raised intra-abdominal pressure in critically injured patients? Canadian journal of surgery. Journal canadien de chirurgie 2000. Can J Surg 2000;43(3):207-11.

Kirkpatrick AW, Roberts DJ, De Waele J, Jaeschke R, Malbrain ML, De Keulenaer B et al. Intra-abdominal hypertension and the abdominal compartment syndrome: updated consensus definitions and clinical practice guidelines from the World Society of the Abdominal Compartment Syndrome. Intensive care medicine 2014. Intensive Care Med 2013;39:1190-1206 (PubMed year field 2014).

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on a soft abdomen to exclude IAH/ACS in ventilated, massively resuscitated or post-laparotomy patients.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Tense abdomen with oliguria, rising airway pressures or hypotension → measure bladder pressure immediately; IAP >20 mm Hg with new organ failure = abdominal compartment syndrome, surgical consult.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Examination was performed by a blinded clinician; no interobserver statistics reported in the abstract. Prevalence quotes: '47 (32%) were more than 10 mm Hg and 16 (11%) were more than 15 mm Hg' (Abstract, Results).

extraction_notes: Anchor PMID 10851415 confirmed (Kirkpatrick 2000); PMC3695163 exists but has no OA body text, so estimates come from the abstract, which reports sens/spec/PPV/NPV/accuracy for two thresholds. Reported numbers are measurement-level (147 measurements in 42 patients, clustered), which the CI-free values do not account for. LRs computed (flagged). The index test is the examiner's global judgment of 'elevated' abdominal pressure rather than a specific 'tense/distended' descriptor; the maneuver is the same bedside judgment. Thresholds (>10 and >15 mm Hg) predate and differ from the WSACS 2013 definitions (IAH ≥12 mm Hg; ACS >20 mm Hg with organ dysfunction; WSACS anchor PMID 23673399 confirmed, cited as guideline). Sugrue et al. Arch Surg 2002 'Clinical examination is an inaccurate predictor of intraabdominal pressure' (unverified recall) was not retrievable by title search and is not cited; Sugrue 1995 (PMID 7749700) concerns IAH and renal impairment, not exam accuracy, and is not cited.
